chapter.title: Names and Messages
chapter.para: This chapter describes how a Rexx program reaches .NET: namespaces and types by name, and the members of a type or an object through Rexx messages.

section.title: Namespaces and Types
section.para: &net; is the root of .NET's namespaces. A message to it, or to a namespace, is the name of a sub-namespace or of a type in it: .net~System is the namespace System, a instance, and .net~System~Text~StringBuilder the type System.Text.StringBuilder, a instance. The names are caseless. The framework's assemblies are loaded when a name first needs them: .net~System~Text~RegularExpressions~Regex needs no load.

What a name resolves to never changes, so it is remembered: a namespace or a type reached by name is the same object each time, and the second .net~System~Math asks .NET nothing. A name that is not found is not remembered: after a load it may be there.

Where a name is not enough, takes a type's full name as a string, with C# aliases (int, string, bool...), generic types in C# syntax, array types, and nested types (Outer+Inner); or an open generic type and its type arguments. gives a namespace by its exact name, and loads an assembly that is not part of the framework, by name or by the path of its .dll.

example.title: Namespaces and types
example.programlisting:
ns = .net~System~Text say ns say ns~StringBuilder (.net~type("System.Text.StringBuilder") == ns~StringBuilder) say .net~type("int") .net~type("string[]") say .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>") open = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List`1") say .net~type(open, .net~type("double"))
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: a NetNamespace (System.Text) a NetType (System.Text.StringBuilder) 1 a NetType (System.Int32) a NetType (System.String[]) a NetType (System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<System.String, System.Int32>) a NetType (System.Collections.Generic.List<System.Double>)

section.title: Messages to Types and Objects
section.para: A message to a type reaches its static members, and new calls a constructor; a message to an object reaches its instance members:

table.title: Rexx messages and the .NET members they reach

row.entry: a property or field read, or a method called with no arguments; an event gives a NetEvent ()
a method call (), or an indexed property read
a property or field write; the member must exist
the indexer, or an array's element ()
a constructor of the type t
a static member of the type t
an event handler added or removed ()

section.para: Only public members are reached. An object of a type that is not public (an iterator made by C#'s yield, an internal implementation of a public interface) has the members of its nearest public base class and of the public interfaces it implements, as C# sees it through its declared type. Protected members are reached only by the methods of a Rexx class that extends the type ().
Method calls chain, as in C#: sb~Append("a")~Append(42) appends twice, because Append returns the StringBuilder itself.

section.title: Names in Any Case
section.para: ooRexx uppercases every message name, so the bridge looks members up without regard to case: sb~length, sb~LENGTH and sb~Length are the same message. If two public members differ only in case, the one that starts with an uppercase letter wins (.NET's convention for public names); a tie that this does not break is an error naming both.

Exact access takes the name as it is written, in its case, with no guessing: calls a method, reads a property or field, and writes one. They also reach a member whose name is a Rexx method of NetObject or Object (). lists the public members' names.

example.title: Names in any case, and exact access
example.programlisting:
sb = .net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new("abc") say sb~length sb~LENGTH .net~get(sb, "Length") say .net~invoke(sb, "Insert", 0, "x")~ToString .net~set(sb, "Capacity", 50); say sb~Capacity signal on syntax say .net~get(sb, "length") -- exact: there is no "length" syntax: say condition("O")~code condition("O")~additional[2]
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Rexx's Own Methods
section.para: A NetObject is a Rexx object, so it has the methods of Rexx's Object class (class, isA, objectName, hasMethod...), and those of NetObject (). A Rexx method wins over a .NET member of the same name, with six exceptions, names that .NET uses often: start, send, copy, run, request and string go to the .NET member when the object (or type) has one, and to Rexx's method otherwise. So stopwatch~Start, process~Start, .net~System~IO~File~Copy(a, b) and .net~System~String (the type) all reach .NET. Any other name that Rexx also has is reached with or .
say o and concatenation use makeString, which shows what a proxy is (a NetObject (System.Text.StringBuilder #12)); to get .NET's text, send o~ToString.

example.title: Rexx's methods and .NET members of the same name
example.programlisting:
w = .net~System~Diagnostics~Stopwatch~new w~Start -- .NET's Start say w~IsRunning say .net~System~String~Concat("a", "b") -- the type System.String say w~class~id -- Rexx's class
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Overloads
section.para: A .NET method may have several overloads: methods of the same name with different parameters. Rexx strings carry no type, so the bridge chooses the overload as C# would for arguments of unknown type: the candidates are those of the name that take that number of arguments (counting params arrays and optional parameters), and a candidate fits if every argument converts to its parameter (). Among those that fit, the cheapest wins: an exact type (a NetObject of the parameter's type, or a forced type) before a widening or reference conversion, before a conversion from a Rexx string; among strings, a string parameter first, then numbers by width (int before long before double), then the rest. As in C#, a candidate that needs an empty params array or a default value filled in loses a tie to one that takes the arguments as they are.
A tie is an error that names the candidates; so is an argument list that no candidate accepts. Forcing one argument's type settles either: .net~int64(x), .net~as(x, "short") ().

example.title: Overloads chosen by the arguments
example.programlisting:
m = .net~System~Math say m~Max(3, 7.5) m~Max(.net~int64(3), 7) say .net~System~Convert~ToString(255, 2) .net~System~Convert~ToString(255, 16) signal on syntax say m~Max(.net~as(1, "object"), 2) syntax: parse value condition("O")~message with first ";" -- (then the candidates) say first
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Generic Methods
section.para: A generic method's type arguments are inferred from the arguments, as C# infers them, also through base types and interfaces (First<T>(IEnumerable<T>) takes a List<int>): a .NET object gives its type, a forced value its forced type, a Rexx Array the common type of its items, and a Rexx string System.String, as Rexx strings have no other type to infer from (.net~int32(5) makes it an int). Constraints that fail drop the candidate; on a tie a non-generic method wins, as in C#.

Type arguments that cannot be inferred are given in the name, in C# syntax, through : .net~invoke(e, "Empty<int>"), or as a message whose name is a string: e~"Empty<int>". A method whose type arguments cannot be inferred says so, and shows that form.

example.title: Generic methods
example.programlisting:
e = .net~System~Linq~Enumerable l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<int>")~new do i = 1 to 5; l~Add(i); end say e~Sum(l) e~Max(l) e~First(l) -- inferred: int, from the List say e~Repeat("ab", 2)~makeArray~makeString("L", " ") say .net~invoke(e, "Empty<int>")~makeArray~items
::requires "net.cls"

section.para: Extension methods (LINQ's Where, Select...) are static methods of their class, and are called as such: .net~System~Linq~Enumerable~ToList(seq), not seq~ToList.

section.title: Structs
section.para: A struct (a value type, as DateTime, Point or KeyValuePair) comes to Rexx as a boxed copy, a NetObject. Its properties and methods work as for any object; but setting a field, or calling a method that changes the struct, changes that copy, not the value that .NET holds: form~Location~X = 5 moves nothing (C# does not even compile it). Set the whole value instead: form~Location = .net~System~Drawing~Point~new(5, y). Passing a struct to .NET passes a copy, as in C#.

section.title: Assemblies
section.para: Types are found in the assemblies already loaded, then in the framework's assemblies (those of every shared framework the runtime was started with: on Windows the desktop framework too), loaded on demand: by a namespace's name (System.Text.RegularExpressions), by a type's name (System.Console), and, as a last resort, by an index of the framework's public types, read once from their metadata without loading them (System.Timers.Timer is in System.ComponentModel.TypeConverter.dll).

Any other assembly is loaded with : by the path of its .dll, or by name. A name that the runtime does not know is looked for as name.dll in the current directory, then next to the bridge: an assembly that was in .NET Framework's global cache and is a NuGet package today (System.Speech) is found by copying its .dll there. A NuGet package's assembly is loaded by the path of its .dll; the assemblies it depends on that are not part of the framework are not looked for by themselves: load them first, the same way.
